rv.q: He’s found a way to scramble enough of the structure of a boy-meets-girl romantic drama to thrill, if not leave a deep impression.
The play sustains our interest thanks to the memorable characterizations and superb work by the two actors.
As these co-dependents, Lee and Teague give bravura performances which remain high-powered throughout.
Lee understands the assignment, showing flashes of wit and compassion despite her character's dazed existence.
Despite the production’s high-proof stagecraft, at times I couldn’t help feeling myself staggering through the play’s 100 minutes.
As Him, Teague gives a literally sobering performance, finding a self-assured manner when off the bottle, then crumbling under the weight of his compulsions.
The result is more irritating than cathartic.

A review quote not exceeding 90 characters: Blackout Songs is surprisingly seductive, drawing the audience in with the charisma of its two leads even as it depicts how frightening, unmooring, and destructive alcohol dependence can be.
The effect is initially fascinating, but ultimately exhausting — like enduring the slurry rant of that friend who’s had two too many and now just won’t shut up.
Lee and Teague offer a vivid portrait of codependency and mutual enablement in White’s drama, at the Robert W. Wilson MCC Theater.
It’s a beguiling, heart-wrenching ninety-minute pas de deux as two lost souls try to find love and escape together.
White’s acting showcase stands as a riveting piece of theatre that lingers long after the curtain call.

cn.t: This Olivier-nominated two-hander about codependent addicts earns praise as an acting showcase but divides critics on execution. Strong performances can't fully overcome a fragmented, challenging structure that some find seductive and others merely exhausting.
